title: Sheba's Revolt and the Wise Woman of Abel
summary: Before David is even settled back in Jerusalem, a Benjamite named Sheba calls the northern tribes to abandon him. David confines the ten concubines Absalom had violated, orders his new commander Amasa to muster Judah, and when Amasa is slow, sends Abishai after Sheba. Joab murders Amasa on the road, takes back command, and besieges Sheba in the northern town of Abel-beth-maacah, where a wise woman negotiates the town's survival by having Sheba's head thrown over the wall. The chapter ends with a list of David's officials.
story: Absalom's rebellion is over, but its wounds are open. At the end of chapter 19 the men of Israel and the men of Judah quarreled bitterly over who had more right to bring the king home, and Judah's words were harsher. Sheba steps into that gap. His cry, “We have no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse’s son. Every man to his tent, O Israel!” (verse 1), shows how fragile the union of north and south still is. The same cry will be raised again, almost word for word, when the kingdom finally splits under Solomon's son (1 Kings 12:16). This chapter also settles, for now, who controls David's army. David tried to replace Joab with Amasa, Absalom's former commander, and Joab answers with a knife. The list at the end of the chapter shows Joab back over the whole army, a man David cannot control and will warn Solomon about on his deathbed.
historical:
The events belong to the later years of David's reign, which most scholars date to about 1010 to 970 BC. The kingdom was still a loose union of tribes held together by the person of the king, and the old line between the northern tribes (often simply called Israel) and Judah in the south ran deep. Sheba was a Benjamite, from Saul's tribe, and resentment over the loss of the crown from Saul's house surfaces more than once in these chapters (compare Shimei in 16:5-8).

Abel-beth-maacah lay in the far north of Israel, near Dan and the headwaters of the Jordan, close to the border with the Aramean state of Maacah. Its name means something like meadow of the house of Maacah. It later fell to the Aramean king Ben-hadad (1 Kings 15:20) and to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III (2 Kings 15:29). The list of officials in verses 23-26 repeats, with changes, the one in 8:15-18. Adoram, over the forced labor, appears to be the same man called Adoniram under Solomon (1 Kings 4:6) and Adoram under Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:18), which suggests that conscripted labor began under David, not only under Solomon.
cultural:
Siege warfare in this period meant building a ramp of earth and stones against a city wall so that soldiers could bring battering equipment up to it, which is what Joab's troops do in verse 15. A siege could last weeks and end in the destruction of the whole town. Abel's rescue comes through a figure Israel respected: the wise woman, a recognized counselor whose words carried weight in a community (the woman of Tekoa in chapter 14 is another). She appeals to Abel's reputation as a place where people went to seek counsel, to its status as a mother in Israel (a leading town with dependent villages around it), and to the idea of the land as the LORD's inheritance, which Joab would be destroying.

The concubines in verse 3 were secondary wives of the king. Absalom had publicly slept with them to claim his father's throne (16:21-22), and in the ancient Near East taking a king's women signaled a claim on his kingdom. David cannot resume relations with them, and he cannot send them away, so they live out their lives as widows in a guarded house, cared for but set aside. The text records it without comment, and the reader feels the cost of Absalom's act falling on women who had no say in it. Joab's greeting, taking Amasa's beard to kiss him, was an ordinary gesture of friendship, which is what makes the murder so treacherous.
literary: The chapter is built as a pursuit with two sharply contrasting encounters. On the road, a man meets a man with a greeting of peace and a hidden blade, and the victim is left wallowing in blood while the army stops to stare. At the wall, a woman meets the same man with words, and a whole town is spared. The narrator lets the contrast speak: violence and wisdom, the dagger and the counsel. The exchange at the wall is written as quick dialogue, with repeated calls to listen. Verse 19 is the heart of her speech, a question that shames the general. The pursuit framework (Sheba's horn in verse 1, Joab's horn in verse 22) opens and closes the story, and the list of officials rounds off the long account of Absalom's revolt and its aftermath that began in chapter 13.

outline.t: Sheba calls Israel away from David
Amasa's delay and Joab's murder of Amasa
The siege of Abel and the wise woman's counsel

doctrines.note: Wisdom in the Old Testament is practical skill for living well, and here it saves lives. The woman of Abel knows her town's history, speaks with authority, and finds the narrow way to justice without slaughter. The chapter prizes that kind of wisdom above force.

The consequences of David's earlier sins keep unfolding: the concubines' confinement is fallout from Absalom's revolt, and Joab's violence goes unpunished because David depends on him. Sin rarely stays with one person; it spreads through a household and a kingdom.

Sheba's cry exposes how easily loyalty to God's chosen king can dissolve into tribal grievance. The unity of God's people under his anointed is a gift that can be lost, as the later split under Rehoboam shows.

words.note: Beliyyaal, worthlessness, here in the phrase a man of worthlessness, rendered worthless man. It describes someone lawless or destructive. The word later became Belial, a name for Satan in some Jewish writings and once in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 6:15), but here it is a moral judgment on a troublemaker, not a demonic title.

Nachalah, inheritance: land passed down in a family, and by extension Israel as the LORD's own possession. Sheba uses it to say the north has no stake in David's house (verse 1); the wise woman uses it to call Abel part of the LORD's inheritance (verse 19). The same word frames both a rebellion and a plea for mercy.

Bala, to swallow up, used for the earth swallowing Korah or a destroying enemy. The woman asks why Joab would swallow up the LORD's inheritance, and Joab throws the word back in his doubled denial, “Far be it from me to swallow up or destroy!” It pictures total destruction, the thing she persuades him not to do.

christ: This chapter's connection to Christ is thematic, not predictive. It shows a kingdom that can't hold together under David's house and a king who can't restrain the violence done in his name. Sheba's cry that there is no share in David is the opposite of the later prophetic hope that God's people would be gathered again under one shepherd from David's line (Ezekiel 37:22-24). The New Testament sees that gathering in Jesus, the son of David, who unites not only Israel and Judah but Jew and Gentile in one body (Ephesians 2:14-16). And where Joab kills a rival under cover of a kiss, the Gospels record another kiss of betrayal (Luke 22:48), with the difference that the betrayed one gave himself up for those who betrayed him.

hard.q: Why does Joab murder Amasa and face no consequence, and why does the wise woman hand over Sheba's head?
hard.a: The text does not approve of Joab. It describes the killing in grim detail and later has David name Joab's murders of Abner and Amasa as crimes Solomon must answer (1 Kings 2:5-6). Joab goes unpunished in David's lifetime because David's hold on power depends on him, a weakness the narrative exposes rather than excuses. The woman's choice is harder. Sheba was a rebel under sentence for raising his hand against the king, and by the standards of the time his death was a legal penalty; she spared a whole town by giving up the one man the army sought. Readers differ on how to weigh it. Some see a hard but just act of wisdom that saved many innocent lives; others note that the story, like much of 2 Samuel, reports a violent world honestly without holding every act up as a model.

questions: Sheba turned an old grievance into a rebellion. Where have you seen resentment between groups exploited by someone who stood to gain from it?
The wise woman saved her town with words, knowledge of her community's history, and courage. What does that kind of wisdom look like in a conflict you face?
The concubines paid for sins that were not theirs. Who in your community bears the cost of other people's choices, and what would care for them look like?
